content: The variability in blood transfusion practices across and within countries can be attributed to several factors, with one key determinant being the inconsistent adoption and implementation of best practices informed by high-quality research. Strategies to implement such research aim to minimize the risks associated with blood transfusion, particularly in light of the variability in laboratory screening practices for transfusion-transmitted infections. Efforts to improve the safe and appropriate use of blood transfusion include the development of evidence-based guidelines, which are essential for educating clinicians who order blood components. These guidelines also serve as a foundation for establishing systems to ensure the appropriate clinical use of blood, such as clinical audits. In 2013, 126 countries reported having national guidelines for the clinical use of blood. Across WHO regions, the percentage of countries with such guidelines varied: 74% in Africa, 57% in the Americas, 70% in the Eastern Mediterranean, 77% in Europe, 72% in South-East Asia, and 68% in the Western Pacific. Data from 109 countries revealed that hospital transfusion committees were present in 39% of hospitals performing transfusions. The regional distribution of hospitals with such committees was as follows: 14% in Africa, 20% in the Americas, 57% in the Eastern Mediterranean, 92% in Europe, 57% in South-East Asia, and 25% in the Western Pacific. However, fewer countries provided information on whether hospitals participated in systems for reporting adverse transfusion events or conducted clinical audits. In 97 countries, systems for reporting adverse transfusion events were present in 17% of hospitals in Africa, 91% in the Americas, 32% in the Eastern Mediterranean, 99% in Europe, 59% in South-East Asia, and 37% in the Western Pacific. Clinical audits were conducted in 7% of hospitals in Africa, 38% in the Americas, 24% in the Eastern Mediterranean, 83% in Europe, 58% in South-East Asia, and 21% in the Western Pacific. Haemovigilance, a critical component of blood safety systems, involves monitoring and evaluating adverse events related to the blood supply and transfusion services to improve safety and outcomes. In 2013, 39% of countries reported having a national haemovigilance system. Europe had the highest percentage of countries with such systems (77%), followed by South-East Asia (46%), the Eastern Mediterranean (35%), the Western Pacific (32%), Africa (26%), and the Americas (14%). Regarding plasma utilization, 51 countries reported arrangements for using plasma collected domestically for fractionation. Of these, 37 countries used domestic or contract fractionation, eight sold plasma to fractionators and purchased plasma-derived medicinal products (PDMPs) from the market, and six employed both strategies. One country, Croatia, reported closing its fractionation plant and changing its strategy for PDMP provision. Globally, between 23 and 28 million liters of human plasma are fractionated annually, though WHO data suggests a lower volume due to incomplete reporting. A total of 96 countries reported importing all PDMPs, while 17 countries reported not using any PDMPs during the reporting period. Analysis by collection method showed that 41% of plasma sent for fractionation was recovered plasma, with significant contributions from the Western Pacific Region. In terms of governance, 122 countries (68%) had a national blood policy in 2013, and 96 countries (53%) had a multiyear national strategic plan for blood safety. Additionally, 127 countries (71%) had a unit within the Ministry of Health responsible for governing blood-related activities, and 88 countries (49%) had a national blood committee to assist in policy formulation and standard-setting. Specific legislation covering blood transfusion safety and quality existed in 105 countries (58%). Financial mechanisms for blood services varied. In 2013, 32% of countries reported having a specific government budget line for blood transfusion services, while 16% had a cost recovery system. Across WHO regions, Europe had the highest percentage of countries financing blood services through cost recovery schemes (67%), while in Africa, government budget allocations were the primary mechanism (48%). International financial and technical support played a significant role in some regions. For example, 78% of reporting countries in Africa received financial support from international agencies, compared to 9% in the Americas and 25% in the Eastern Mediterranean. Similarly, 83% of African countries received technical support, compared to 44% in the Americas and 35% in the Eastern Mediterranean.
